latin.44: Ad alias rationes quod spectat, utinam eas suus autor suscepisset tuendas, qua mihi videtur esse et sapientia et eloquentia, praestitisset id, quam ego, multo melius. Prima sic se habet, referente D. Garissolio; Manuscriptum enim ex quo sunt desumptae non habeo. Fidem esse penes eum oportet. Nemo nescit illud, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, apud bonos autores, vel denotare finem rei, τὸ τέλος, vel causam antecedentem, ut apud Synesium, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ γεννάδιον ἔχαρε. Cum igitur finis hoc loco denotari non possit, sequitur ut causa antecedens designetur, et vertatur eo quod, vel propterea quod. Quid respondet D. Gar? Hoc unum, ἐπί junctum cum relativo ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, quanquam aliquando finem, aliquando causam antecedentem notet, tamen frequentissime vim habere praepositionis ἐν. Marc. 2. 4. ἐφ᾽ ᾧ κατέκειτο in quo jacebat &c. Sed quid hoc est, nisi aberratio ab argumento? Nam in argumento agebatur de vocibus ἐφ᾽ ᾧ absolute positis, hoc est, absque expresso antecedente ad quod pronomen ᾧ referatur. Cum enim est in proximo antecedens ad quod refertur, quis unquam eas vertendas putavit eo quod vel propterea quod? Hic autem ponuntur absolute, quod enim proxime antecedit est nomen θάνατος bis usurpatum, ac ante illud ἁμαρτία; ad neutrum referri constat. Praecedit quidem Genitivus ἀνθρώπου hominem; Sed quominus ad eum referri possit, obstant interjecta nomina, immo commata.
latin.45: Secunda ratio. Si Apostolus de imputatione cogitasset, locus hic unice flagitabat, ut eam diserte commemoraret: et debuit dicere ἐν ᾧ, non ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, quia res ardua est, et a communi sensu abhorrens, itaque oportuit eam clare exprimere, ne quis de ea dubitaret. Respondet primo, an imputari aliena peccata a communi sensu abhorreat, jam supra disputatum est. Immo abhorret, ut imputentur aliquibus prorsus innocentibus, ut ob aliena imputata hi puniantur ea poena quae sit vere peccatum, eosque faciat inhaerenter peccatores, ut hac imputatione fiant rei mortis aeternae, alioqui non rei. Hoc, inquam, a sensu communi, a Scriptura, et ratione, ab ipsoque conscientiae sensu mihi videtur vehementer abhorrere. Quid? nonne si quis diceret, alia Adami, aut aliorum Patriarcharum peccata nobis omnibus imputari, is videretur a communi sensu abhorrentia dicere? Sit aliqua alieni peccati non injusta imputatio, an id probatum est de omni, ac nominatim de ista tali, primi peccati actualis imputatione immediata, qua nulla mihi fingi posse videtur injustior?
latin.46: Resp. 2. Hic notandam confessionem viri Docti: Si dictum fuisset ἐν ᾧ, imputationem peccati inde manifeste concludi potuisse, quippe diserte commemoratam. Ita enim instantiam posterioris scripti contra hanc imputationem damnat, ubi pretenditur, etiamsi vertas, in quo, inde tamen nihil colligi posse pro causa imputationis. Miror ἀγχίνοιαν viri docti, non videntis autorem illius rationis non ex sua, sed ex eorum, contra quos disputabat, mente sic fuisse locutum. Ita enim argumentantem decet ex Adversariorum hypothesibus, potius quam ex suis ipsius, disputare, alioqui nihil promoturum.
latin.47: Resp. 3. vix ferendum videri, quod dicitur, si Paulus imputationem docere voluisset, debuisse potius ἐν ᾧ dicere quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. Qui enim nos sumus, qui Apostolo praescribere audeamus loquendi rationem, et formulas, praesertim cum ἐν et ἐπί tam frequenter eundem sensum et significationem habeant? Clementer quaeso: abhorret enim sine dubio vehementer ab hujusmodi arrogantia rationis illius autor. Non praescribit Apostolo loquendi rationem et formulas, sed ab ejus sapientia et prudentia, quam summam fuisse constat, ducit argumentum. Quaerebatur quid Apostolus significare voluit verbis ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον? Aiunt quidam eum significare voluisse, primum Adami peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse, et quidem immediate. Quoniam ergo hanc mentem Apostolo, non dicam praescribunt, sed tamen, quia ita ipsis placet, tribuunt; atque ad eam mentem verba ejus minus accommodata paululum inflectunt, ἐπί pro ἐν positum nulla reddita ratione, affirmantes. Ille objicit, hoc sapientiae Apostolicae minus convenire. Cum enim ejusmodi doctrina sit admodum ardua, et a sensu communi abhorrens, et alibi non doceatur in Scriptura, consentaneum erat, ut saltem hoc uno in loco doceretur aperte, et verbis disertis, aut saltem iis, quae falso quidem, sed tamen pro disertis ab iis habentur qui a nobis in hac causa dissentiunt. Si saltem dixisset ἐν ᾧ, non fuisset opus recurrere ad enallagem praepositionis ἐπί positae pro ἐν, et minus fuisset ambigua vocum ἐν ᾧ significatio: multo enim rarius, quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, significant eo quod, quatenus &c. Cum ergo Apostolus consulto dicere maluerit ἐφ᾽ ᾧ quam ἐν ᾧ, ac, quantum fieri potuit, ab illis removerit, et pluribus interpositis separaverit nomen ἀνθρώπου; atque ita impediverit ne ad id tanquam antecedens relativum ᾧ referretur, cur sine necessitate, sine ratione, malumus eius verbis et verborum collocationi vim aliquam inferre, ut id dicere aliquomodo videantur quod ex eis colligi nequit, quam retenta verborum ἐφ᾽ ᾧ proprietate, et Apostolico commatum situ eam sententiam verborum eius admittere, quam in se veram esse nemo non Pelagianus negare potest? Sed quid, inquit, impediet, quominus Pelagius aut Socinus eadem ratione objicere possint; Si Scriptura docere voluisset, vel peccatum generatione propagari, vel Christum esse Mediatorem merito et satisfactione; id expressuram fuisse, vel exprimere debuisse verbis claris et perspicuis, cum res sit ardua, nec satis ad communem hominum sensum accommodata? Omnino nihil impediet quominus hoc possint objicere, si velint, Pelagii et Socini sequaces; Sed nihil impediet etiam, quominus objicientibus respondeamus, non id quod vult D. G. nostrum non esse, Deo loquendi rationes et modos praescribere: Hoc enim, cum Dei mens et sententia versatur in quaestione, sophisticum videri possit; Sed quod res est, id neque a sensu conscientiae ullo modo abhorrere, et tam disertis ac claris verbis in Scriptura exprimi, ut, nisi iis magna vis afferatur, in alium sensum detorqueri nequeant.
latin.48: Tertia ratio. Locus non postulat ut ita vertatur: cum enim causa certa sit, cur Apostolus dixerit, mortem in omnes homines pervasisse, nempe quia omnes peccaverunt, quid opus est confugere ad causam incertam et remotam, idque contra verborum vim naturalem? Respondet quatuor: sed, quia vim argumenti non perceperat, ἀποσχεδιάζει. Dixit Apostolus, mortem in omnes homines pervasisse: causa sine dubio est quia omnes peccaverunt. Sed quod peccatum intelligi debeat quaeritur. Alii peccatum intelligi volunt habituale omnibus inhaerens, alii peccatum actuale Adami omnibus ordine naturae priusquam vitiosi sint imputatum. Peccatum habituale inhaerens ab Adamo in omnes propagatum causa est certa, hoc est, confessa ab omnibus orthodoxis. De eo enim vitio quin sit, et causa sit mortis; quippe vere peccatum, vere reos mortis nos efficiens, nulla est inter nos controversia. Id enim est communi confessione fidei verbis clarissimis et disertissimis confirmatum. De peccato vero actuali Adami, an ante corruptionem imputetur, et an illa imputatio sit causa cur in omnes mors pervaserit, res certa non est et liquida: id enim est quod nunc inter nos controvertitur. Rursus vitium unicuique nostrum inhaerens causa est mortis nostrae propinquior, quam primum Adami peccatum actuale, quod nobis imputatum dicitur, non modo prius ordine natura quam essemus corrupti, sed etiam aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse et vivere incepissemus. Itaque cum duae illae causae inter se conferuntur, illa est certa, quia non controversa, haec incerta, quia controversa: illa est proxima in eodem cum suo effectu, hoc est, morte, subjecto, haec remota, quia in alio subjecto, a nobis non modo natura generantis ordine, sed tempore etiam valde remota, ac inter quam et mortem interposita est causa propinquior, nimirum corruptio. Jam, opinor, Lector, aberrant viri docti responsiones ipse per te intelligis. Cum enim certum sit ac nullo modo inter nos controversum, omnibus inhaerere peccatum quod meretur mortem, et ob quod omnes moriuntur, cur de eo peccato verba Apostoli, quibus causa mortis omnium hominum continetur, omnes peccaverunt, non accipimus? Cur eo peccato, quasi nullum esset, insuper habito, confugimus ad aliud imputatum, quod et controvertitur, et ab illo effectu est remotius, praesertim verbis Apostoli et verborum situ repugnantibus?

pass_a.44: Ad alias rationes quod spectat — utinam suus autor (sapientia+eloquentia) suscepisset tuendas; praestitisset multo melius quam ego. Prima sic se habet referente D. Garissolio (manuscriptum desumptarum non habeo; fidem penes eum). Nemo nescit: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ apud bonos autores vel finem rei (τὸ τέλος) vel causam antecedentem denotat — ut apud Synesium ἐφ᾽ ᾧ γεννάδιον ἔχαρε. Finis hic denotari non potest → causa antecedens designatur → vertatur eo quod / propterea quod. D. Gar respondet unum: ἐπί + relativum ὅς/ἥ/ὅ aliquando finem aliquando causam notat, sed frequentissime vim praepositionis ἐν (Marc. 2.4 ἐφ᾽ ᾧ κατέκειτο in quo jacebat). Placeus: aberratio ab argumento — agebatur de ἐφ᾽ ᾧ absolute positis (absque expresso antecedente ad ᾧ). Ubi proximum antecedens adest, quis unquam vertit eo quod/propterea quod? Hic absolute: proxime antecedit θάνατος bis + ante illud ἁμαρτία; ad neutrum referri constat. Praecedit Genitivus ἀνθρώπου; sed interjecta nomina immo commata obstunt quominus ad eum referatur.
pass_a.45: Secunda ratio [Garissoles]: Si Apostolus de imputatione cogitasset — locus unice flagitabat diserte commemorare; debuit dicere ἐν ᾧ non ἐφ᾽ ᾧ; res ardua + a communi sensu abhorrens → clare exprimere ne quis dubitet. Placeus Respondet primo: an imputari aliena peccata a communi sensu abhorreat — jam supra disputatum. Immo abhorret: imputentur aliquibus prorsus innocentibus → ob aliena imputata puniantur poena quae sit vere peccatum + faciat inhaerenter peccatores → hac imputatione rei mortis aeternae (alioqui non rei). Hoc abhorret a sensu communi + Scriptura + ratione + ipso conscientiae sensu (vehementer). Quid? alia Adami / Patriarcharum peccata nobis omnibus imputari → abhorrentia a communi sensu. Sit aliqua alieni peccati non injusta imputatio — an probatum de omni, nominatim de primi peccati actualis imputatione immediata (qua nulla injustior fingi posse)?
pass_a.46: Resp. 2 — notandam confessionem viri Docti: Si dictum fuisset ἐν ᾧ → imputationem peccati manifeste concludi potuisse (diserte commemoratam). Ita damnat instantiam posterioris scripti contra hanc imputationem: etiamsi vertas in quo, nihil colligi posse pro causa imputationis. Miror ἀγχίνοιαν viri docti: non videt autor illius rationis locutus ex eorum mente contra quos disputabat, non ex sua. Argumentantem decet ex Adversariorum hypothesibus potius quam ex suis ipsius disputare — alioqui nihil promoturum.
pass_a.47: Resp. 3 — vix ferendum: si Paulus imputationem docere voluisset, debuisse potius ἐν ᾧ quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. Garissoles: Qui nos sumus Apostolo praescribere loquendi rationem/formulas? ἐν + ἐπί frequenter eundem sensum. Placeus clementer: autor rationis abhorret ab hujusmodi arrogantia; non praescribit sed a sapientia/prudentia Apostoli (summa) ducit argumentum. Quaerebatur: quid ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον significare voluit? Aiunt: primum Adami peccatum actuale omnibus imputatum immediate. Mentem Apostolo tribuunt (non dicam praescribunt) + verba minus accommodata inflectunt (ἐπί pro ἐν, nulla ratione). Ille objicit: minus convenit sapientiae Apostolicae — doctrina ardua, a sensu communi abhorrens, alibi non in Scriptura → consentaneum aperte/diserte hic doceri. Si ἐν ᾧ dixisset: non opus enallage ἐπί→ἐν; minus ambigua ἐν ᾧ; ἐφ᾽ ᾧ rarius = eo quod/quatenus. Apostolus consulto ἐφ᾽ ᾧ maluit quam ἐν ᾧ; removerit + separaverit ἀνθρώπου pluribus interpositis; impediverit relativum ᾧ. Cur sine necessitate vim inferre verbis/collocationi vs retenta ἐφ᾽ ᾧ proprietate + Apostolico commatum situ admittere sententiam quam nemo non Pelagianus negare potest veram? Garissoles Pelagius/Socinus tu quoque: si Scriptura docere voluisset peccatum generatione / Christum Mediatorem merito+satisfactione → verbis claris. Placeus: sequaces possunt objicere; respondemus non 'nostrum non est Deo praescribere' (sophisticum cum Dei mens in quaestione) sed rem: non abhorret a conscientiae sensu + tam disertis verbis exprimitur ut nisi magna vis afferatur detorqueri nequeant.
pass_a.48: Tertia ratio: locus non postulat ita vertatur — causa certa cur Apostolus dixerit mortem in omnes pervasisse = quia omnes peccaverunt; quid opus confugere ad causam incertam+remotam contra verborum vim naturalem? Garissoles respondet quatuor; quia vim argumenti non perceperat → ἀποσχεδιάζει. Dixit Apostolus mortem pervasisse; causa = omnes peccaverunt; sed quod peccatum? Alii: habituale omnibus inhaerens; alii: actuale Adami ordine naturae priusquam vitiosi sint imputatum. Habituale inhaerens ab Adamo propagatum = causa certa/confessa orthodoxis; vitium vere peccatum vere reos mortis → nulla controversia; confessio fidei clarissimis verbis. Actuale Adami ante corruptionem imputatum + causa mortis pervasionis = non certa/liquida (nunc controvertitur). Vitium unicuique inhaerens = causa mortis propinquior quam actuale imputatum (prius ordine natura + millibus annorum ante esse/vivere). Conferuntur: illa certa/non controversa + proxima eodem subjecto cum morte; haec incerta/controversa + remota alio subjecto (natura+tempore) + corruptio interposita. Lector: aberrant viri docti responsiones per te intelligis. Cum certum omnibus inhaerere peccatum merens mortem ob quod moriuntur — cur verba Apostoli omnes peccaverunt de eo peccato non accipimus? Cur eo peccato insuper habito quasi nullum, confugimus ad aliud imputatum controversum+remotius, verbis Apostoli + verborum situ repugnantibus?

44: As for the other reasons, would that their own author had undertaken to defend them — by the wisdom and eloquence with which he seems to me to be marked — he would have performed that far better than I. The first stands thus, as D. Garissoles reports it; for I do not have the manuscript from which they were taken. Faith must rest with him. Nobody is ignorant that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, among good authors, either denotes the end of a thing (τὸ τέλος) or an antecedent cause, as in Synesius, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ γεννάδιον ἔχαρε. Since therefore an end cannot be denoted in this place, it follows that an antecedent cause is designated, and that it be rendered "in that," or "because." What does D. Garissoles answer? This one thing only: that ἐπί joined with the relative ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, although it sometimes marks an end and sometimes an antecedent cause, nevertheless most frequently has the force of the preposition ἐν. Mark 2:4: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ κατέκειτο, "in which he was lying," and so on. But what is this except a wandering from the argument? For in the argument the discussion was of the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ placed absolutely — that is, without an expressed antecedent to which the pronoun ᾧ is referred. For when there is a near antecedent to which it is referred, who ever thought those words ought to be rendered "in that" or "because"? But here they are placed absolutely: for what immediately precedes is the noun θάνατος used twice, and before that ἁμαρτία; and it is established that they are referred to neither neuter. The genitive ἀνθρώπου, "man," does indeed precede; but intervening nouns — nay, even commas — stand in the way of referring the relative to him (Romans 5:12).
45: Second reason. If the Apostle had thought of imputation, this place uniquely demanded that he commemorate it expressly; and he ought to have said ἐν ᾧ, not ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, because the matter is hard and abhorrent from common sense, and therefore he ought to have expressed it clearly, lest anyone doubt concerning it. He answers first: whether the imputing of alien sins abhors from common sense has already been disputed above. Nay, it abhors that they be imputed to some who are altogether innocent, so that on account of alien things imputed these men are punished with a punishment which is truly sin and makes them inheringly sinners, so that by this imputation they become liable to eternal death who otherwise would not be liable. This, I say, from common sense, from Scripture, and from reason, and from the very sense of conscience, seems to me to abhor vehemently. What? If someone should say that other sins of Adam, or of the other Patriarchs, are imputed to us all, would he not seem to say things abhorrent from common sense? Let there be some imputation of an alien sin that is not unjust: has that been proved of every imputation, and namely of this such immediate imputation of the first actual sin, than which none more unjust seems to me able to be feigned?
46: Response 2. Here the confession of the learned man is to be noted: that if ἐν ᾧ had been said, the imputation of sin could have been concluded thence manifestly, as expressly commemorated. So he condemns the instance of a later writing against this imputation, where it is pretended that even if you render "in which," still nothing can be gathered thence for the cause of imputation. I marvel at the shrewdness (ἀγχίνοιαν) of the learned man, who does not see that the author of that reason spoke thus not from his own mind but from the mind of those against whom he was disputing. For so it befits one who argues to dispute from the adversaries' hypotheses rather than from his own; otherwise he will advance nothing.
47: Response 3. It seems scarcely bearable that it is said: if Paul had wished to teach imputation, he ought rather to have said ἐν ᾧ than ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. For who are we who dare prescribe to the Apostle a manner of speaking and formulas — especially when ἐν and ἐπί so frequently have the same sense and signification? Gently, I ask: without doubt the author of that reason abhors vehemently from arrogance of this kind. He does not prescribe to the Apostle a manner of speaking and formulas; he draws an argument from his wisdom and prudence, which is established to have been the highest. It was asked what the Apostle wished to signify by the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (Romans 5:12). Some say he wished to signify that Adam's first actual sin was imputed to all men, and that immediately. Since therefore they attribute this mind to the Apostle — I will not say they prescribe it, but because it so pleases them — and toward that mind they bend a little his words, less accommodating as they are, affirming that ἐπί is put for ἐν with no reason given. He objects that this less befits Apostolic wisdom. For since a doctrine of this kind is very hard, and abhorrent from common sense, and is not taught elsewhere in Scripture, it was fitting that at least in this one place it be taught openly and in express words — or at least in those words which, though falsely, are nevertheless held as express by those who dissent from us in this cause. If at least he had said ἐν ᾧ, there would have been no need to recur to an enallage of the preposition ἐπί put for ἐν, and the signification of the words ἐν ᾧ would have been less ambiguous: for much more rarely than ἐφ᾽ ᾧ do they signify "in that," "inasmuch as," and so on. Since therefore the Apostle deliberately preferred to say ἐφ᾽ ᾧ rather than ἐν ᾧ, and as much as could be done removed them from those antecedents, and by several things interposed separated the noun ἀνθρώπου, and so hindered the relative ᾧ from being referred to it as antecedent — why without necessity, without reason, do we prefer to force some violence upon his words and upon the collocation of the words, so that they seem somehow to say what cannot be gathered from them, rather than, retaining the propriety of the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ and the Apostolic situ of the clauses, admit that sense of his words which in itself no one but a Pelagian can deny to be true? But what, he says, will hinder Pelagius or Socinus from objecting by the same reason: if Scripture had wished to teach either that sin is propagated by generation, or that Christ is Mediator by merit and satisfaction, it would have expressed it, or ought to have expressed it, in clear and perspicuous words, since the matter is hard and not enough accommodated to the common sense of men? Altogether nothing will hinder the followers of Pelagius and Socinus from being able to object this if they wish; but nothing will hinder us either from answering those who object — not what D. Garissoles wants, that it is not ours to prescribe to God manners and modes of speaking (for this, when God's mind and sentence is turned in the question, can seem sophistic); but what the fact is: that it neither abhors in any way from the sense of conscience, and is expressed in Scripture in words so express and clear that, unless great force is brought upon them, they cannot be twisted into another sense.
48: Third reason. The place does not demand that it be so rendered: for since there is a certain cause why the Apostle said that death pervaded into all men, namely because all sinned (Romans 5:12), what need is there to flee to an uncertain and remote cause, and that against the natural force of the words? He answers four things: but because he had not perceived the force of the argument, he improvises (ἀποσχεδιάζει). The Apostle said that death pervaded into all men: the cause without doubt is because all sinned. But which sin ought to be understood is the question. Some want habitual sin inhering in all to be understood; others Adam's actual sin imputed to all in the order of nature before they are vicious. Habitual inhering sin propagated from Adam into all is a certain cause — that is, confessed by all the orthodox. For concerning that vice — that it exists and is a cause of death, being truly sin and truly making us liable to death — there is no controversy among us. That is confirmed by the common confession of faith in the clearest and most express words. But concerning Adam's actual sin — whether it is imputed before corruption, and whether that imputation is the cause why death has pervaded into all — the matter is not certain and liquid: for that is what is now controverted among us. Again, the vice inhering in each of us is a nearer cause of our death than Adam's first actual sin which is said to be imputed to us — not only earlier in the order of nature than we were corrupted, but even by some thousands of years before we began to be and to live. Therefore when those two causes are compared with each other, that is certain because not controverted, this uncertain because controverted; that is proximate in the same subject with its effect — that is, with death — this remote because in another subject, from us not only by the order of generating nature but also by time very remote, and between which and death a nearer cause is interposed, namely corruption. Now, I think, Reader, you yourself understand through yourself the learned man's aberrant responses. For since it is certain and in no way controverted among us that there inheres in all a sin that merits death and on account of which all die, why concerning that sin do we not take the Apostle's words in which the cause of the death of all men is contained — "all sinned"? Why, that sin being set aside as if it were none, do we flee to another imputed sin, which both is controverted and is remoter from that effect — especially when the Apostle's words and the situ of the words resist?
